Kindling The four-week launch plan for a consumer app · by the Ignura crew · 3 October 2026 · 8 min read In this post Before week one: pick the date Week 1: the teardown and the plan Week 2: polish, screenshots and the landing page Week 3: the launch film and the UGC shoot Week 4: line it up, then launch After launch: keep it burning Only got two weeks? The whole plan, on one page Share the short version Pick the launch date first, then work backwards. Leave room for App Store review. Week 1: the teardown and the plan. Week 2: polish, screenshots, landing page. Week 3: the launch film and the UGC shoot. Week 4: line it up and launch. Pick two or three channels and do them properly, rather than seven badly. Only two weeks? Keep the screenshots, a one-page site, five UGC videos and a tight launch day. Shrink the film. Skip deep polish. in a hurry? start here Four weeks is the sweet spot for launching a consumer app. It’s long enough to make things you’re proud of and short enough that nobody loses the plot. Give a launch two months and it turns into a “project” with a Notion page nobody opens. Give it a week and you ship a screen recording with a stock track under it. This is the plan we run for an Ignite launch, written out so you can run it yourself. Steal all of it. Before week one: pick the date# Everything works backwards from launch day, so pick it first and say it out loud to someone who’ll hold you to it. Pick a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Mondays are for inboxes, and Fridays are for leaving early. Check it doesn’t clash with a bank holiday, a big Apple event or a competitor’s launch you already know about. Leave room for review. App Store review is often quick, but “often” isn’t a plan. Submit your release build at least a week before launch day and set it to manually release this version, so it’s approved and waiting rather than going live at 3am on its own. Check Google’s rules if you’re on Android. Newer personal Google Play developer accounts have to run a closed test before they can publish to production (at the time of writing: 12 testers for 14 days). That alone is longer than two weeks, so start it now. the date first. everything else hangs off it. Careful: The date is the plan A launch without a date isn’t a launch, it’s a mood. If the date moves, move it once, on purpose, and tell everyone the same day. Week 1: the teardown and the plan# The goal of week one is to know exactly what you’re launching, who it’s for, and what you’ll say. No pixels yet. Use your app like a stranger. Delete it, reinstall it, sign up with a new email and go through onboarding without skipping anything. Write down every moment you hesitate. This is the same thing we do in a free teardown, and it’s always humbling. Write the one sentence. What it is and who it’s for, in words your mum would understand. “X for Y” is fine. If the team can’t agree on the sentence, the screenshots, the film and the creators definitely won’t. Find the hero moment. Every good consumer app has one screen where people go “oh, nice”. The card flipping over, the map filling in, the photo turning into something. That moment is the star of your screenshots, your film and your UGC. If it’s buried three screens deep, moving it forward is your most important design job. Pick your channels. Two or three, done properly. For most consumer apps that’s TikTok (or Reels), X and Product Hunt. Each one needs real work, so a channel you can’t feed is better dropped now than abandoned on the day. Book people now. Creators, a motion designer, whoever’s helping with the film: they need lead time. Week three is too late to start asking. By Friday you should have: A launch date, with the build submitted no later than a week before it The one sentence everyone agrees on The hero mome

Give a launch two months and it turns into a “project” with a Notion page nobody opens. Give it a week and you ship a screen recording with a stock track under it. This is the plan we run for an Ignite launch, written out so you can run it yourself. Steal all of it. Before week one: pick the date# Everything works backwards from launch day, so pick it first and say it out loud to someone who’ll hold you to it. Pick a Tuesday, Wednesday or Thursday. Mondays are for inboxes, and Fridays are for leaving early. Check it doesn’t clash with a bank holiday, a big Apple event or a competitor’s launch you already know about. Leave room for review. App Store review is often quick, but “often” isn’t a plan. Submit your release build at least a week before launch day and set it to manually release this version, so it’s approved and waiting rather than going live at 3am on its own. Check Google’s rules if you’re on Android. Newer personal Google Play developer accounts have to run a closed test before they can publish to production (at the time of writing: 12 testers for 14 days). That alone is longer than two weeks, so start it now. the date first. everything else hangs off it. Careful: The date is the plan A launch without a date isn’t a launch, it’s a mood. If the date moves, move it once, on purpose, and tell everyone the same day. Week 1: the teardown and the plan# The goal of week one is to know exactly what you’re launching, who it’s for, and what you’ll say. No pixels yet. Use your app like a stranger. Delete it, reinstall it, sign up with a new email and go through onboarding without skipping anything. Write down every moment you hesitate. This is the same thing we do in a free teardown, and it’s always humbling. Write the one sentence. What it is and who it’s for, in words your mum would understand. “X for Y” is fine. If the team can’t agree on the sentence, the screenshots, the film and the creators definitely won’t. Find the hero moment. Every good consumer app has one screen where people go “oh, nice”. The card flipping over, the map filling in, the photo turning into something. That moment is the star of your screenshots, your film and your UGC. If it’s buried three screens deep, moving it forward is your most important design job. Pick your channels. Two or three, done properly. For most consumer apps that’s TikTok (or Reels), X and Product Hunt. Each one needs real work, so a channel you can’t feed is better dropped now than abandoned on the day. Book people now. Creators, a motion designer, whoever’s helping with the film: they need lead time. Week three is too late to start asking. By Friday you should have: A launch date, with the build submitted no later than a week before it The one sentence everyone agrees on The hero mome
